name: Zygomatic sandwich osteotomy

lead: A zygomatic sandwich osteotomy cuts the cheekbone and separates the pieces, then fills the gap with a graft or spacer so the bone is wider. The aim is to broaden the cheek and change how the midface looks, which hardmaxxing forums discuss as a way to get more cheekbone width.

Surgeons describe it in reviews of facial skeletal augmentation. One facial plastic surgeon, Dr. Eppley, states that it widens the cheek sideways and does not add forward projection, which in his view only an implant provides.

paras: It is performed by facial plastic or craniofacial surgeons under anaesthesia, with the bone cut, separated and filled. People considering it in hardmaxxing communities compare it with cheek implants, filler and cheekbone reduction. The term also describes an unrelated dental technique on the jaw ridge, so searches mix the two.

It is major facial bone surgery. Surgical literature on facial osteotomies describes general risks such as infection, graft problems, asymmetry, numbness and long recovery, and surgeons advise consultation with a qualified facial surgeon.

web.title: Can a zygomatic osteotomy increase anterior cheek projection? - Eppley Plastic Surgery

chain: Graft fills the gap to widen the bone
angle.text: The surgery changes bone width at the cheek. Surgeon commentary says it increases lateral width rather than forward projection.

lead: A zygomatic sandwich osteotomy is a facial skeletal surgery in which the zygoma, or cheekbone, is cut and spread apart and the gap filled with a graft, so the bone is built up between the cut pieces [1][2]. It was described in the surgical literature as a route to malar augmentation, alongside synthetic implants [1].

In hardmaxxing discussions it is raised as a way to change cheekbone width and midface structure. Surgeon commentary distinguishes what it can and cannot do: Dr. Eppley states that the procedure widens the cheek laterally and does not pull the cheekbone forward, and that only an implant adds projection [2].

The name 'sandwich osteotomy' is also used in oral surgery for a different procedure that raises the height of the jaw ridge for dental implants. Most published research under that name concerns the jaw, not the cheekbone [3][4].
infobox: Increased lateral width, not forward projection [2]

paras: A sandwich osteotomy cuts a bone and places a graft or biomaterial between the pieces. A 2004 review of skeletal volume enhancement covers synthetic implants, the zygomatic sandwich osteotomy for malar augmentation and distraction osteogenesis [1].

Dr. Eppley, a facial plastic surgeon, writes on his practice site that a zygomatic sandwich osteotomy widens the cheek and does not add forward projection, comparing it with malar rotation, which narrows the cheek and likewise does not add projection [2]. He states that no bony cut effectively pulls the cheekbone forward and that an implant is needed for that effect [2]. This is one surgeon's view rather than a consensus statement.

In oral and maxillofacial surgery, sandwich osteotomy usually means a segmental cut of the jaw ridge with a graft placed in the gap to add height before dental implants. Systematic reviews and trials examine it in the posterior mandible and anterior maxilla [3][4]. Those findings concern the dental ridge and do not describe the cheekbone.

Reviews of the jaw version describe complications such as neurosensory changes and graft or segment problems [3]. For the cheekbone, the general surgical risks of facial bone cuts apply, and surgeons advise evaluation by a qualified facial surgeon.

No studies found on the cheekbone version in large trials. A 2004 review discussed the zygomatic sandwich osteotomy for malar augmentation [1]. Systematic reviews and randomised trials of sandwich osteotomy concern the jaw ridge for dental implants, a different procedure [3][4].
